newsitem.title: FRANCE: Star-studded gala, Wenders film mark Cannes' 50th.
newsitem.headline: Star-studded gala, Wenders film mark Cannes' 50th.

text.p: The Cannes festival marks its 50th anniversary on Sunday with a star-studded gala at which Wim Wenders unveils his thriller "The End of Violence", the latest in this year's competition diet of brooding films.

French President Jacques Chirac, assuming a high profile during a tightly contested parliamentary election campaign, showed up in Cannes for lunch with members of the festival jury and a chance to mug for the cameras with big film stars.

But the Gaullist head of state was due to leave Cannes before the evening jamboree during which some 30 previous winners of Cannes' top Golden Palm prize will award Swedish master Ingmar Bergman a special Palm of Palms.

The reclusive Bergman has refused entreaties to attend, but his actresses Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann will be present at the ceremony dedicated to Italian director Marco Ferreri who died in Paris on Friday of a heart attack.

Stars flocking to the French Riviera resort for the celebrations include Gina Lollobrigida, Claudia Cardinale, Anjelica Huston, Jane Campion, Robert de Niro, Johnny Depp, Sylvester Stallone, Pedro Almodovar, Roman Polanski, Francis Coppola, Martin Scorsese and Gerard Depardieu.
Geena Davis, Costa Gavras, Robert Altman, Kenneth Branagh, Milos Forman, and Vittorio Gassman will also be present at the ceremony, followed by a 600-strong dinner offered by jewellers Cartier.

Cannes veteran Wenders, voted best director in 1987 for "Wings of Desire" and on the jury two years later, screens before his peers a tale of state-sanctioned violence and intrusive police surveillance of Los Angeles public life.
Violence, said the bespectacled Wenders, 52, "is conceived, produced and distributed in this city. Los Angeles has a very particular rapport with violence."

Gabriel Byrne and Andie MacDowell, whom Wenders discovered in Cannes in "Sex, Lies and Videotape", star in the movie featuring a former NASA computer programmer who tries to stop the FBI using a surveillance system he developed in an attempt to put an end to violence in the city.
Bill Pullman plays a successful Hollywood producer of violent movies who is forced to go into hiding after the programmer crosses his path.

"All the characters are deeply affected by violence -- and violence happens -- but only before or after: we never indulge in exploiting violence or showing it," Wenders said of his first English-language production since Golden Palm winner "Paris, Texas".

"Though we wanted the film to be about violence, we didn't want violence to be part of the film's language...To describe a disease, you have to risk catching it," said Wenders, who wrote the script in just six weeks and shot the $6.5 million film in 28 days.

Wenders insists that he has now abandoned the New German Cinema of his roots: "I don't look back on that road anymore. I feel that I had over-explained it at a certain time, and over-explained the importance of the American dream and the American movie. When I went back to Europe, it seems now to me like it's all a lot of...".
